---
title: "Adding the GitHub interface to your RStudio"
format: html
---


The steps below are adapted from the wonderful book “Happy Git and GitHub for the useR” by Jenny Bryan: <https://happygitwithr.com/>

1.	Register a GitHub account – DONE

2.	Install (newest versions of) R and RStudio – DONE

3.	Install git: <https://happygitwithr.com/install-git/>
    a.	The exact instructions will depend on your operating system – click on the link above and follow the steps for your system.
    b.	If you are required to use the Terminal, you can use it within RStudio.

4.	Introduce yourself to git: <https://happygitwithr.com/hello-git>
    a.	Start by installing two helpful packages: `usethis` and `gitcreds`
    b.	Then, type in:
    `library(usethis)`
    `use_git_config(user.name = "Jane Doe", user.email = "jane@example.org")`
    NOTE: Substitute your name and email for the “Jane Doe”

5.	Set up a Personal Access Token (__PAT__): <https://happygitwithr.com/https-pat>
    a.	Go to <https://github.com/settings/tokens> and click __Generate new token__.
    From the drop-down menu, pick  __Generate new token (classic)__.
    You should see something similar to @fig-generate-token:  
    
    ![Give a description of what the token is for, change the expiration to __90 days__ (to ensure it remains valid for the duration of the course), and select scopes: `repo`, `user`, and `workflow`.](images/generate-token.png){#fig-generate-token}
    
    b.	Look over the scopes; I highly recommend selecting __repo__, __user__, and __workflow__. 
    c.	For the Expiration, pick 90 days, so the token doesn’t expire during this course.
    d.	Click __Generate token__.
    e.	Copy the generated PAT to your clipboard.
        Or leave that browser window open and available for a little while, so you can come back to copy the PAT.
    f.	Provide this PAT next time a Git operation asks for your password (which might not happen in this class).
    g.	Get out ahead of this and store the PAT explicitly right now. In R, call `gitcreds::gitcreds_set()` to get a prompt where you can paste your PAT: `gitcreds::gitcreds_set()`.
    Paste the PAT in response to the dialogue in the console.

You should be able to work with GitHub now, i.e. "push" and "pull". 

6.	Connect to our course GitHub repository:
    a.	In the steps below, we will be setting up a new subfolder within your data-science folder.
    This new subfolder will be called `data-science-for-health-bms-STUDENT-2526`.
    If you already have a folder called this (which may have happened if you successfully followed the workflow in Week 1), rename it to ‘old-notes’ or similar.
    If you do this, your folder structure would look as @fig-ds-folder-structure:
    
    ![Cloned repo. You should have a folder `data-science` that contains week by week content folders.](images/ds-folder-structure.png){#fig-ds-folder-structure}

    b.	In your internet browser, go to our course GitHub repository, which is: <https://github.com/DDI-Talent/data-science-for-health-bms-STUDENT-2526> (you may have this bookmarked, as you have downloaded files from there before)
    c.	Once on the page, click on the green <> Code button. Make sure that the HTTPS protocol is selected, and copy the repo URL from the dialogue box, like this:
    d.	In RStudio, go to File > New Project > Version Control > Git. In “Repository URL”, paste the URL that you’ve just copied
    e.	Accept the default project directory name, `data-science-for-health-bms-STUDENT-2526`, which coincides with the GitHub repo name.
    f.	Make sure that the new project directory is saved within your data-science folder.
    g.	I suggest you check “Open in new session”, as that’s what you’ll usually do in real life.
    h.	Click “Create Project”.
